action_criteria.rationale: Autonomic dysfunction is common in severe GBS and can cause bradyarrhythmias and blood pressure lability; tracheal suctioning is a recognised trigger of bradycardia.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not treat with corticosteroids: oral corticosteroids are strongly advised against and IV methylprednisolone is not recommended [EAN_PNS_2023].
Do not give IVIg directly after plasma exchange, and do not give a second IVIg course [EAN_PNS_2023, Walgaard_2021].
Do not start IVIg without checking renal function.
Do not use succinylcholine if reintubation is needed: denervated muscle risks severe hyperkalaemia.
required_recommendations: Start IVIg 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days (2 g/kg total, about 27 g/day at 68 kg): she cannot walk, is ventilated and is within 2 weeks of onset; plasma exchange 200-250 mL/kg over 5 sessions is an equal alternative, but sepsis, blood pressure lability and the ACE inhibitor are relative cautions here [EAN_PNS_2023].

Continue ICU care with mechanical ventilation; measure MIP and FVC daily on the ventilator with checks of bulbar function, cough and secretions, and do not extubate while bulbar and respiratory weakness persist or progress [Lawn_2001, EAN_PNS_2023].
Continuous cardiac telemetry with arterial blood pressure monitoring for autonomic instability, with attention to bradycardia during suctioning.

Once the CSF (acellular, negative Gram stain, culture, bacterial PCR panel and HSV PCR) and the brain MRI exclude meningitis and encephalitis, stop vancomycin, ampicillin and acyclovir and treat the community-acquired pneumonia alone.

Manage the QT risk of azithromycin (QTc 464 ms with dysautonomia): repeat the ECG daily, keep potassium and magnesium in range and add no other QT-prolonging drug; if the QTc lengthens further, change the atypical pneumonia cover to an agent without QT effect.
Keep metformin withheld and control glucose with insulin while she is critically ill and receiving nephrotoxic drugs; follow creatinine during IVIg.
Start mechanical and pharmacological DVT prophylaxis appropriate for an immobilised, ventilated patient.

avoided_actions.rationale: Echocardiography is not indicated in typical GBS; reserve for pre-existing cardiac disease or unexplained hemodynamic instability after autonomic causes are excluded.
Two head CTs were already unremarkable; a third CT adds nothing, and MRI is the study that answers the encephalopathy question.
Functional / metabolic brain imaging adds no value in a peripheral demyelinating syndrome.
Vascular imaging is not needed: diffusion-weighted MRI is the study that excludes an infarct behind the asymmetric facial and arm signs, and the deficits are bilateral and areflexic.

accepted: Guillain-Barré syndrome (severe acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy) during community-acquired pneumonia

differential.diagnosis: Infectious or post-infectious encephalitis / ADEM (including Mycoplasma-associated)
differential.key_features: Fever and encephalopathy raised it, but the brain MRI shows no parenchymal signal change or enhancement, the CSF is acellular with negative PCRs, and the EEG shows only diffuse reactive slowing; consciousness recovered once ventilation corrected the hypercapnia.

Reduced consciousness with limb weakness raises it, but eye movements are full, there is no ataxia or ophthalmoplegia, the brainstem is normal on MRI and the drowsiness is explained by hypercapnia (PaCO2 61 mmHg) and sepsis.
Cannot be excluded at presentation: progression over 6 days fits GBS; reconsider if progression continues beyond 8 weeks or treatment-related fluctuations recur.
Neck stiffness and fever prompted empirical cover; CSF with 2 cells/mm3, negative Gram stain, culture, bacterial PCR panel and HSV PCR, and a normal MRI exclude them.

The left facial and arm weakness triggered a stroke alert, but the weakness became bilateral and areflexic with flexor plantars, the facial weakness is lower motor neuron and bilateral, and diffusion-weighted MRI shows no infarct.
No tick bite or endemic exposure; the CSF has no lymphocytic pleocytosis.
No sensory level, areflexia rather than hyperreflexia, flexor plantars, and facial and bulbar involvement place the lesion in the peripheral nerves.
Weakness ascended from the legs with distal sensory symptoms, pupils are reactive, and the NCS is demyelinating.

key_clinical_evidence: Rapidly ascending, relatively symmetric four-limb weakness with areflexia and bilateral facial weakness over 6 days, with CSF albuminocytological dissociation (protein 118 mg/dL, 2 cells/mm3) and a demyelinating NCS, meets Brighton level 1 once meningitis, encephalitis and stroke are excluded [Brighton_2011].

Fever, encephalopathy, neck stiffness and asymmetric signs make GBS less likely and must each be explained [EAN_PNS_2023]: here the acellular CSF with negative microbiology, the normal brain MRI and an EEG with diffuse slowing only exclude meningitis, encephalitis and stroke.

In a patient with ascending weakness, drowsiness can be the presentation of neuromuscular respiratory failure: the pre-intubation FVC of 13.2 mL/kg with PaCO2 61 mmHg explains the decline in consciousness [Lawn_2001].
The antecedent infection is a history finding; serology is not needed for the diagnosis, and a positive IgM does not prove the trigger.
Dysautonomia in GBS adds to the QT effect of macrolides and fluoroquinolones; the interaction check before treatment is part of the work-up here.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The fever is the community-acquired pneumonia. The decline in consciousness fits hypercapnic respiratory failure (PaCO2 61 mmHg before intubation) with sepsis-associated encephalopathy: she is awake and following commands once ventilated, the CSF is acellular with negative microbiology, the MRI is normal and the EEG shows only diffuse slowing.
red_herrings.data_point: A week of fever (38.6 C) with confusion progressing to unresponsiveness
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggest meningoencephalitis as the cause of both the encephalopathy and the weakness.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The CSF has 2 cells/mm3 with a negative Gram stain, culture and bacterial PCR panel, which excludes meningitis; neck stiffness and neck pain can accompany GBS (radicular inflammation).

The facial weakness is lower motor neuron and bilateral, worse on the left; facial and limb involvement in GBS can be asymmetric. The weakness became bilateral and areflexic with flexor plantars, and diffusion-weighted MRI shows no infarct.
red_herrings.data_point: Left facial droop with greater left arm weakness that triggered a stroke alert
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggest an acute right hemisphere stroke.

sequence_constraints.reason: Creatinine, potassium and magnesium are read before the interaction check, because the renal risk of IVIg with acyclovir and vancomycin and the QT risk of azithromycin depend on them.

interactions: Azithromycin: known risk of QT prolongation and torsades de pointes; the effect is additive with other QT-prolonging drugs, including fluoroquinolones such as levofloxacin. Avoid combining QT-prolonging drugs and monitor the QTc, potassium and magnesium (relative caution when the baseline QTc exceeds 460 ms).
Intravenous immunoglobulin with acyclovir and vancomycin: each can cause acute kidney injury and the risk is additive; ensure hydration and follow creatinine daily (relative caution).
Lisinopril (ACE inhibitor) with albumin-replacement plasma exchange: bradykinin-mediated flushing and hypotension; withhold the ACE inhibitor for at least 24 hours before an exchange.
Metformin: risk of lactic acidosis if renal function falls; keep withheld while nephrotoxic drugs are given and renal function is at risk.
general.proposed: Intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange, with current azithromycin, ceftriaxone, vancomycin, ampicillin, acyclovir and fentanyl; home lisinopril and metformin (held)
general.summary: Eight agents reviewed against intravenous immunoglobulin and plasma exchange.
warnings: Intravenous immunoglobulin: thrombotic events are more frequent in older patients and in those with diabetes or hypertension; check renal function before each dose.
Fentanyl: respiratory depression; relevant at extubation in neuromuscular respiratory weakness.

labs.interpretation: Leukocytosis (WBC 14.8). Sodium 132 (low). Glucose 186 (elevated). Albumin 3.2 (low). CRP 88.4 and procalcitonin 2.8 (elevated). Renal function, liver tests, CK and platelet count within reference. Blood cultures no growth at 48 h; urine Legionella antigen and HIV Ag/Ab negative.

results.finding: Guidelines for adults with GBS who cannot walk unaided advise IVIg 2 g/kg over 5 days within 2 weeks of onset or plasma exchange within 4 weeks, with no preference between them; corticosteroids are not advised.
A second IVIg course in patients with a poor predicted prognosis did not improve outcome and caused more serious adverse events.

general.summary: IVIg or plasma exchange is advised for adults with GBS unable to walk unaided; neither is preferred, and a second IVIg course is not advised [EAN_PNS_2023, Walgaard_2021].

specialized_test.impression: Study performed on day 2. 1. Prolonged distal motor latencies and slowed motor conduction velocities in the demyelinating range in median and peroneal nerves, with reduced CMAP amplitudes. 2. Absent F-waves and H-reflexes. 3. Absent sural and reduced median sensory responses. 4. Needle EMG: reduced recruitment without active denervation. Findings are consistent with a sensorimotor polyradiculoneuropathy with demyelinating features. Clinical correlation recommended.

metadata.difficulty_description: GBS presenting as febrile encephalopathy during community-acquired pneumonia: meningitis, encephalitis and stroke must be excluded before the albuminocytological dissociation and demyelinating NCS are read as GBS; QT-prolonging antibiotics with dysautonomia.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 7 required actions, 3 red herrings; the encephalopathy, neck stiffness and asymmetric signs must each be excluded with CSF, MRI and EEG.
metadata.revision_reason: Reviewer 2 GBS audit: spine MRI is optional and limited to five cases with a concrete cord, traumatic, postoperative or infiltrative alternative; generic hidden MRI reports removed.

patient.chief_complaint: One week of fever with confusion and inability to walk, first treated as meningoencephalitis, followed by rapidly ascending weakness and intubation.

medications.indication: Type 2 diabetes (home medication, held since admission)
Pneumonia and empirical meningitis cover (dose increased Day 1)
Analgesia and light sedation on the ventilator (started Day 1)

patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. G. is a 67-year-old woman with hypertension and type 2 diabetes who had a 1-week history of cough and intermittent fever. Three days before this admission she was seen in the emergency department for presumed community-acquired pneumonia and discharged on levofloxacin; at that visit she mentioned tingling in both feet that had started the day before. She returned 3 days later with worsening fever (38.6 C), generalized weakness, inability to walk, confusion and difficulty expressing herself. She denied sick contacts, recent travel, tick bites or animal exposures. There were crackles at the left lung base, and a chest X-ray showed patchy left lower lobe consolidation. Levofloxacin was stopped and she was admitted on ceftriaxone and azithromycin for community-acquired pneumonia. On admission (Day 0) she was mildly inattentive but oriented to person, place and time, moved all four limbs but could not lift her arms more than 10 inches against gravity, and could not stand unaided. A head CT was unremarkable. On Day 1 she was oriented only to person, had neck stiffness and incomprehensible speech but followed simple commands, and a left facial droop with greater left arm weakness triggered a stroke alert; a second head CT was unremarkable. Later on Day 1 she became drowsy with shallow breathing, then unresponsive; she was intubated and transferred to the MICU. Vancomycin, ampicillin, high-dose ceftriaxone and acyclovir were started for possible meningoencephalitis, and lumbar puncture was deferred during intubation and transfer. Home lisinopril and metformin have been held since admission. Neurology is consulted on Day 2 for rapidly ascending weakness with depressed reflexes.

neurological_exam.additional: Examined on Day 2 in the MICU, intubated, on a light fentanyl infusion. No rash. No sensory level on the trunk.
neurological_exam.coordination: Cannot be assessed because of weakness.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal and reactive. Eye movements full on command; no ptosis. Bilateral lower motor neuron facial weakness, worse on the left (incomplete eye closure on the left, weak right eye closure). Gag reflex reduced. Speech not assessable (intubated).
neurological_exam.mental_status: Day 2: awake on light sedation, responds to her name and follows simple commands. On Day 1 before intubation: oriented only to person with incomprehensible speech, then unresponsive.
neurological_exam.motor: Day 2: hip flexion and knee extension 1/5, ankle dorsiflexion 1/5 bilaterally; shoulder abduction, elbow flexion and grip 3/5 bilaterally. Neck flexion 3/5. On Day 0 she moved all limbs but could not lift her arms more than 10 inches, and on Day 1 the left arm was weaker than the right.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Day 2: absent at the knees and ankles, trace (1+) at the biceps and brachioradialis bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor.
neurological_exam.sensory: Limited by intubation: withdraws to pain in all four limbs; vibration reduced at both great toes.

physical_exam.general: Weight 68 kg, height 155 cm. Vital signs are those recorded on admission (Day 0).
physical_exam.respiratory: Day 2: intubated on assist-control ventilation; coarse crackles at the left base.
